content.thinking:
I'm planning out a Warcraft-style gray wolf design with chunky heroic proportions, hand-painted gradients, and accessories like a studded leather collar, aiming to capture that saturated, worn-in fantasy art style.

I'm working out the actual proportions — roughly 0.8-0.85m shoulder height, 1.1m body length, with tail bringing total to around 1.6-1.7m — and sketching out a joint hierarchy for the skeleton, starting with hips as the root and building spine, neck, head, and tail chains from there using forward-positioned coordinates.

Working out the leg geometry: placing shoulder and hip joints, giving paws a chunky radius, and defining front leg segments (shoulder, elbow, wrist, paw) with lengths that create the right bend direction for a digitigrade canine stance.

With 3 spans between 4 points, I need 4 names: shoulder, elbow, wrist, and paw as the tip, with the tip aimed along the path's end tangent. The chain's role is "leg," and I still need to figure out which parent joint it attaches to on the spine.

Front legs should parent to the chest joint while hind legs parent to the hips. I'm passing a point array directly as the path for each leg chain, since a polyline with joints at span starts works fine here, even with fillets smoothing the corners. For the hind leg, I'm laying out hip, knee, hock, and paw with segment lengths like thigh 0.30 and shin 0.30.

Checking the geometry: with the hind leg root near the hip and target near the ground, the reach of 0.88 comfortably exceeds the 0.68 needed, giving a plausible pose — thigh angled forward-down, shin back-down, and the metatarsus nearly vertical with the hock sitting around 0.35 in height. For the front leg, similar math works out with the wrist landing around 0.20 and the elbow kicking slightly back, confirming the limb lengths and target positions are reasonable.

Now I'm sketching the chunky paw design: a flattened sphere body with small toe capsules and claw spikes, sized and positioned so the paw bottom just barely sinks below the floor plane (within an acceptable 2% margin for a model roughly 1.1 units tall). I'm also setting leg tube radii, tapering thick upper legs down to the wrist for that stylized, oversized Warcraft-style silhouette.

Shifting to the torso, I'm laying out a spine chain from hips to chest using a curved path that captures a deep chest and narrow waist, with specific joint positions for hips, spine segments, and chest. I'm designating hips as the root joint of the skeleton, with the spine chain branching from that same root position up toward the chest, keeping in mind the rule that there must be exactly one root joint with no parent.

I'll define the spine path with four points rising from the hips up to the chest, mapping to spine1/spine2/spine3 joints with the final point serving as spine3's aim target, then continue with the neck chain starting near that upper spine point.

The neck path climbs from the chest through two intermediate points up to the head base, reflecting an alert wolf pose with the neck raised about 45 degrees and the head angled slightly forward. I'm mapping this to neck1/neck2/neck3 joints with a head joint parented to neck3, aimed slightly downward-forward, and I'm now double-checking overall height proportions — head top near 1.25, ears up to 1.40 — against a realistic wolf shoulder height, adjusting slightly larger for the chunky stylized look.

Now I'm thinking through how to build the body mesh itself, sweeping it along the spine/hips joints from rump to chest using a series of path points with increasing height and forward z-position, letting the neck sweep begin inside the chest for a seamless transition, and considering loft stations with width/height per station rather than shift offsets.

Working out rump-to-chest body stations...

Continuing the body section sizing, giving the rump a slightly lower profile than the withers to match a wolf's natural back slope. Now I'm planning the fur details: ruff cards on the neck, chest, and tail plus tufts along the body edges, each drawn as a tapering gradient blade shape.

For coloring, I'll draw the fur tufts in greyscale only, from white at the tip fading to grey at the root, so they can be tinted by a single coat-color paint that multiplies over the drawing—keeping texture consistent across different coat variants. The coat itself gets a hand-painted gradient look: darker grey along the back, warm mid-grey through the body, cream on the belly, with subtle warm highlights on top and cooler shadow tones underneath.

Now I'm defining the actual coat color constants and building a custom paint function that layers noise-based mottling and grain for fur-like streaking, countershading from a dark back tone through mid grey to a cream belly.

I'm now estimating texel density for the paint resolution, weighing 2048 versus 4096 atlas size given total surface area, and leaning toward 2048 since there's plenty of coverage but worried it could overflow and force a halving.

For the coat design, I'm planning a hand-painted gradient look rather than toon shading, with warmer tones on top and cooler underside shading, building this through composable paint functions like a countershade layered over a mottled cream base.

I'm layering the saddle pattern by surface normal — dark on top, mid-gray tan on the sides, cream underneath — to get that classic wolf look, then adding tan-brown accents to the legs using position-based masks for the lower leg regions.

For the legs, I'm distinguishing the front stripe: wolves have that dark "pencil line" running down the front of their front legs, so I'm using the normal vector facing forward to mark that stripe in a darker fur color while keeping the rest of the leg tan, then blending that leg coat into the body coat below the chest line.

Rather than hitting a hard threshold, I'm softening the leg-to-belly transition with a bit of noise so the fur boundary looks jagged and natural instead of a clean cut, writing a small zigzag helper function for that effect. Next I'm moving on to building the head in a bold Warcraft-style silhouette, starting with a scaled sphere for the skull and a frustum shape for the muzzle.

I'm also planning out the remaining head pieces — jaw, fangs, cheek ruffs, ears, and eyes — and thinking the amber wolf eyes should skip the glow effect to avoid looking too flat, instead relying on a painted decal with gradient iris, slit pupil, and a highlight for a more painterly look.

Working out how to place the eye decal directly onto the eyeball sphere rather than using a floating flat plane, since that would look awkward against the curved socket.

I'm thinking through the eye slant direction for wolves—the outer corner sits higher, angling toward the nose at the inner corner. I'll draw a front-facing almond shape and mirror it for the opposite side.

Now I'm working out the decal placement math on the eyeball surface, figuring out how the direction vector and up-axis orientation determine mirroring between the left and right eyes.

For the head, I'm placing the neck joint and using head-local directional coordinates like forward/up/right to position features more intuitively relative to the head's orientation.

Since these are model-space directions rather than bone-aligned ones, I can just compute positions directly in model coordinates using a fixed head origin with offsets, avoiding reliance on the local-frame helper.

Working out skull proportions and placement at the head joint, then shaping the muzzle as a tapered sweep from skull front toward the nose with rounded cross-sections.

Now I'm adding the nose pad as a small dark scaled sphere at the muzzle tip with a subtle highlight, then setting up the separate lower jaw bone hinged at the skull base with its own tapered sweep and pale coloring, plus dark lip edges and fang/incisor teeth geometry.

I'm deciding to keep the mouth closed in the resting pose while letting the jaw open slightly for a snarl expression, then placing the upper and lower canines so they peek just past the lip line, working out exact muzzle sweep coordinates and radii relative to the head center.

Now I'm refining the jaw curve so its top edge touches the muzzle bottom seamlessly, tapering the jaw bottom toward a chin pad, and comparing the chunky head width against the body width to get the proportions right.

Scaling the whole head up by 1.15 for that oversized Warcraft look, I'm placing the brow ridges above the eyes and positioning the eyeballs forward and lateral. Now I'm working out the tall triangular ear outlines.

Positioning the ear with x across the face and thickness along the depth axis, then adding a smaller inner-ear extrude in a lighter fur color nested inside the main ear shape.

I'll paint the ear with a gradient blending from a mid base tone to near-black at the tip, then consider adding small fur tuft cards near the inner ear base and along the neck ruff for texture.

Now I'm sizing the neck and chest ruff cards larger for a mane effect, adding smaller cheek ruff cards on the skull, and planning a Warcraft-style leather collar with rivets — sweeping a lifted loop around the neck joint and scattering brass sphere rivets along it.

I'm also considering adding a buckle plate and a hanging fang pendant to the front of the collar, checking that it fits the "alert gray wolf" aesthetic without going overboard, and double-checking that the neck sweep's loop-cutting plane will correctly intersect the sloped neck joint without missing.

Now I'm figuring out the neck geometry itself: using a sweep along the neck bone chain from chest to head, tapering radii from roughly 0.15-0.16 down to 0.09 at the skull base, and pinning down the exact coordinates where the neck ends and the head joint begins so the skull sits correctly.

Adjusting the neck's curve points to give it a slight S-shape rather than a straight line between chest and head.

Now plotting the tail as a chain hanging from the hips, curving down and back with bushy radii that taper toward the tip, plus darker banding near the end for a wolf-like look.

For tail fur cards, I'm thinking scatter placement with larger tufts flowing down and back along the tail sweep. For the skeleton, I'm reasoning through how the spine's bone list and joint ownership works—each joint claims the path segment based on its projection, with the first joint handling everything before the first span starts.

Now I'm working out leg and shoulder attachment points: front legs parenting to spine3 near the chest, hind legs parenting to the hips, with shoulder joints positioned slightly inside the body mass. To get that heroic, chunky Warcraft-style silhouette, I'm adding sphere/capsule bulges for shoulder pads and haunches, rigged to spine3 and hips respectively, with countershaded coat paint based on surface normals.

I'm setting up the leg chain naming convention using a side multiplier so left limbs get "L" and right get "R", mirroring joint x-positions symmetrically. For paws I'm adding small toe capsules with dark horn-colored claws at the tip joint of each leg chain, though I need to handle the case where the tip joint might be null by falling back to the last joint in the chain.

Now I'm defining the paw shape as a flattened sphere positioned slightly forward and down from the wrist target, plus thin dark grooves between toes and three small capsule bumps for the toe pads at the front of each paw.

Settling on four toes with staggered forward lengths, with inner toes extending farther than outer ones, giving a width around 0.14 that feels proportionate to a chunky paw.

Still placing claws and toe joints...

Checking the paw proportions though, the total length seems too long for the stylized look I want, so I should shrink the toe segment lengths a bit. I'll also add feathering fur cards along the back of the front legs near the elbow sweep area.

For the body, I'm planning several fur card scatters: a general coat layer across the body loft filtered to avoid the belly, a thicker ruff around the neck, and a cream-toned chest ruff where the surface normal faces forward, reading the coat paint color at each card's root for belly/cream blending.

Now I'm thinking about adding weathered details—a scar notch on an ear and a pale scar stripe across the left flank, working out a positional formula using body coordinates to carve three parallel claw-mark lines into the coat paint.

I'm also checking texel resolution so scar lines stay thin enough to read as hand-painted detail at 2048px, and confirming that custom procedural paints don't eat into the flat color budget since they're evaluated per-texel separately from the 64-color limit.

For the coat's shading, I'm adding a lighting helper that darkens colors near the underside and brightens them on top, calling into the base paint resolver and nudging the warm/cool balance depending on the surface normal's vertical component.

Drawing SVG blade shapes...

I need the root anchored at the bottom with the tip pointing up, since that's how the drawing coordinates map to the card orientation. For coloring, I'll have cards read paint from the root, and for surface scattering I'll use a hit filter based on normal direction to control where things get placed, then count triangles per card for the texture budget.

With bend 25, each card needs 2 segments giving 8 triangles, so 400 cards comes to around 3200 triangles, well within the 60k budget—I'm aiming for roughly 1200 cards at 8-16 tris each for about 15k total. I also need to set lean and flow defaults for cards following the body surface, then add a few thin whisker rods near the muzzle and eyebrows using small-radius sweeps, keeping their mesh fine enough to stay under the triangle-edge threshold.

Now I'm working out teeth placement using cone geometry for the fangs—figuring out the orientation so the tip points downward for the upper canines, and positioning them so they sit correctly within the jaw volume relative to the muzzle's z-coordinate and lateral offset.

For the lower canines, I realize they'd mostly be hidden inside the muzzle volume if placed pointing upward, so I'm considering skipping them or only showing a small visible portion, and thinking about whether a slight snarl pose would help make the teeth visible at all.

I'm deciding to skip the tiny incisor row as unnecessary detail, and instead planning a dark lip line sweep along the muzzle-jaw junction to add definition, though I'm uncertain if it'll be visible given how it sits on the surface with the head scaling offsets.

I'll sample path points slightly above the seam on the lower side and define a helper to get muzzle surface points by parameter and angle, using the sweep's angle convention where 90° corresponds to the −X side for a tube running toward +Z.

Working out the angle math: for the left side (+X, s=+1) the lower lip sits around −120°, and the right side mirrors to +120°, so I can generate the lip path with `sweep.line(-s*120, lift)` to trace along the built surface, then sweep a thin tube radius around it for the dark seam detail — and I can reuse `muzzle.at(t, -s*125)` for positioning the fang similarly.

Now I'm placing fangs via `b.stick` oriented along the muzzle surface normal at that lower angle, which naturally points outward and down — correct for fang direction — and embedding them partway into the surface. Then I'm setting up the nose pad position and defining helper constants (HS, HY, HZ, and an `hp` function) to scale head geometry proportionally, starting with the skull sphere part colored with the head coat material.

For the face coat, I'm writing a paint function that colors regions of the head based on relative position: a darker stripe along the bridge of the muzzle, cream tones around the cheeks, lips, and lower muzzle, and grayish tones on the forehead, using normal direction and z/y offsets from the head center to blend the regions smoothly.

I'm also adding a dark eye-mask ring by measuring distance from each eye's center position and darkening nearby surface points, mimicking the eye markings seen on wolves.

Muzzle sides turn cream lower and gray upper for that natural wolf shading effect, with a dark nose, black lips, and dark brow capsules placed above the eyes.

Positioning the brows slanted inward-down for an alert, slightly angry expression, then placing amber eyeballs within socket ellipsoids.

I'm checking whether the eyeball's forward position actually falls outside the skull ellipsoid and into the muzzle root region instead, since the math shows the z-radius ratio exceeding 1 — meaning I need to verify the eye sits correctly where the muzzle sweep begins rather than embedded in the skull itself.

So I'll pull the eyes back toward the skull-muzzle junction and lengthen the skull's z-radius so the eye position lands near the skull surface rather than floating beside the muzzle with no support, adjusting the muzzle start point accordingly to keep it tucked inside the skull.

Now I'm working out the ear placement, angling eyes slightly forward-facing like a real wolf's, and positioning the ear bases near the top-back of the skull by solving the ellipsoid equation to confirm the geometry lines up with the skull's curvature at that point.

Now I'm sizing the ear itself - outline height 0.19, base half-width 0.055, positioned so the top reaches around y≈1.37, giving a total height matching the big Warcraft-style ears I'm aiming for. Next I need to work out the ear's lean angle.

Setting up the orientation vectors for the ear extrusion, making sure x and y stay orthogonal so the outward lean (around 14°) doesn't skew the shape.

Checking the cross product confirms both mirrored cases point outward with +z, so the handedness works correctly for both sides. Now I'm defining the inner ear shape as a smaller extruded outline offset forward and slightly up from the ear base.

Writing ear color gradients...

For the fur, I'm scattering cheek ruff cards on the skull sides and back using a filtering condition, sizing and angling them to lean outward, plus adding small forehead tufts. Now I'm moving on to lofting the body shape and assigning each part.

Working out loft bone weights for the hips and spine chain, and shaping the body radii across stations to tuck the belly near the loin. I'm checking that the spine path and body centers align reasonably, then realizing the neck sweep's round end cap on the chest loft extends too far forward past the intended z-depth, so I need to pull back the last station's position and size to keep the cap from overshooting.

I'm recalculating the body loft stations from rump to chest with adjusted widths and heights so the dome caps land at the right front and rear extents, then checking that the hip bone placement lines up with the first station near the rump.

Now I'm checking neck placement against the chest top, confirming the neck base radius covers the chest properly, and placing the shoulder and haunch mass spheres relative to the body's elliptical cross-section — making sure the shoulder spheres sit slightly outside the torso width while the leg radii stay tucked just inside the body silhouette.

Realizing the total width comes out too chunky for a wolf's narrow frame, I'm tightening the leg x-offset and sphere scale so the body reads leaner while still keeping the stylized broad-shouldered look. Then I'm working out the front and hind leg joint coordinates — elbow, wrist, and paw positions for the front legs, and figuring out how the hind paw should sit slightly behind the hip line to match a natural standing stance with the hock angled backward.

Now I'm plotting the tail's path as a curve from the root near the rump down and back through several control points, giving it a nice bushy droop without touching the floor, then setting up the catmull-rom chain with four spans for the tail bones and a tapering radius profile from thick at the base to a small rounded tip, plus deciding on the underside tail coloring.

Next I'm scattering fur cards along the tail sweep with appropriate size and lean, checking the flow direction follows the tail's downward curve naturally, then moving to the collar — building it as a closed-loop sweep around the neck joint with a leather paint material and a flattened band cross-section rather than a round one.

I'm trying to work out the frame orientation for the loop around the neck — figuring out whether the normal vector aligns with the vertical axis or the horizontal, since that determines which way the flat band faces as it sweeps around.

So with radial normal confirmed, binormal is axial — that settles the radius function: axial half-width 0.03 gives a 6cm wide band, radial thickness 0.011. If I got the axes swapped, it'd come out 2.2cm wide and 6cm thick, which would look wrong.

I'm weighing alternatives like a studded leather collar shape versus building the band as a lathe tube solid around the tilted neck axis, with studs for a chunkier Warcraft-style strap look.

Checking that the lathe ring sits concentric with the neck by matching its axis to the neck joint's tangent direction, estimating the neck radius at that point from interpolated keyframe values (~0.135 at roughly a third of the way along), and allowing a small margin for slight misalignment so it doesn't poke through the geometry.

I'll pass the joint's axis as the direction input for the lathe. For the collar outline I'm sketching a rounded rectangle profile with chamfered corners, then coloring it as mottled brown leather with stitched edges using a paint function.

Adding stitch dashes and studs...

Adding ring studs as 12 small merged spheres, then figuring out the front-facing point on the neck's ring plane to place a buckle plate and hanging pendant, computing the forward radial direction from the neck axis.

Still working out ring orientation...

I think I'd rather hang a fang pendant from the front plate instead — a curved spike dangling on a cord, with its base placed just below and in front of the hit point.

I'm sizing the spike to about 7.5cm length and 1.7cm radius, colored bone-white, and attaching it to the neck bone. But I'm second-guessing the positioning since the neck slants forward and up, so a pendant hanging straight down at the front could end up intersecting the chest rather than hanging freely in space.

I need to work through the actual geometry: tracing the neck's path from chest to head, I'm checking where the collar's frontmost point sits in 3D so I can figure out exactly where the pendant's straight-down drop line will clear the body versus collide with it.

That leaves a small gap with the pendant hanging just in front of the chest, which seems plausible for a cord-hung piece. I need to adjust the angle used to locate the frontmost point of the ring relative to the collar center, since the actual frontmost point sits at roughly elevation -45° rather than -10°.

Calculating the vector from the collar surface points gives an elevation closer to -46°, so I'll use that value and add a null-check since the lookup might return nothing if it misses the surface.

For remaining accessories, I'll keep things simple -- skip extra paint details, use a flat dark horn color for the paw claws, add simple pencil stripes to the front legs, and skip the dewclaw. I'm now considering whether to add fur tufts at the rear elbows.

I'm scattering fur card instances across the legs using a filter on surface normal to catch the back sides of the front legs and the rear thigh breeches, aiming for roughly 900 total cards across the body, neck, chest, head, tail, and legs for a manageable triangle count. Next I'm sketching out the SVG eye texture, defining the almond-shaped eyeliner path with the outer corner raised on the left side.

Continuing with iris, pupil, and lid shading details...

Making the eyeball sphere a dark color so the surrounding area reads as lids, with the cut-away revealing it beneath the amber iris decal, which actually enlarges the eyeliner effect nicely. Now moving on to the nose color.

Still placing nose geometry...

Now I need to set up the jaw joint and figure out its parent relationship within the neck chain.

Adding more joints...

Still writing jaw and teeth geometry...

Adding facial paint details now—whisker dot spots on the muzzle using a cell-based noise pattern, plus battle wear like a scar near the nose bridge and a pale slash mark on the cheek.

Setting up the imports and beginning to write the full implementation code...

Defining helper coordinate functions and color palette constants for the wolf model, then starting on textured fur paints...

Still defining fur colors and shading layers...

I realize the leg boundary is bleeding into the tail region too, turning its lower part tan unintentionally, so I need to restrict the leg coloring to exclude the tail by adding a z-position condition, keeping it confined to actual hind leg placement around z -0.3 to -0.4 while excluding the tail root near z<-0.4.

Writing coat paint function...

Still tuning lighting blend...

Now I'm setting up facial features, defining eye positions and testing distance thresholds to place the dark eye color on the head mesh.

Still defining fur color zones...

Still writing tuft textures...

Now I'm setting up the wolf's skeleton builder, defining the hips joint as root with spine role, then building a spine chain using catmull-rom curve points with three named spine segments parented to the hips.

Next I'm adding the neck chain with four control points curving up and forward, parented to the last spine joint, followed by a head joint placed along the neck curve and aimed with a slight offset.

Checking that the skull back sits behind the neck sweep's end point so the neck radius intersects properly, then building the neck tube with a tapering radius array and default rounded end caps.

Now I'm starting the body loft, defining profile points along the hip-to-spine bone chain with position, width, and height values.

The loft's bone option accepts either a chain or an array of joints, so I'm making sure the hips joint reference matches that type, and noting the neck tube is skinned only to its own chain so posing mismatches with the chest won't matter much. I'm also adding shoulder and haunch bulge spheres on both left and right sides, scaled and positioned relative to the spine and hips joints to give the body some volume.

Now I'm working out the leg geometry, using a limb helper that takes a root position, target position, segment lengths, and bend directions to generate the joint points for each leg, then building chains for the front legs with named joints like shoulder, elbow, wrist, and paw, parented to the spine.

I'm sweeping tapered tube geometry along each chain to give the limbs volume, then setting up the same structure for the hind legs with their own root, target, and segment lengths.

Checking the hind leg's reach against total segment length to make sure the IK target is within range, then doing the same distance check for the front leg.

Working out the knee's forward offset geometrically: with the hip-to-hock vertical span and the two equal segment lengths, I use the chord-height formula to find how far forward the knee should bow, landing on roughly 0.23 forward displacement, which places the knee's z-coordinate near -0.3.

Now checking the hind leg with slightly different segment lengths [0.30, 0.29, 0.24]: the forward offset comes out smaller, around 0.2, putting the knee near z≈-0.1 given the hip and hock positions — this feels reasonable for a wolf's stifle sitting under the flank, though I want the hind paw set further back, so I'll target the hock at z=-0.40. Now moving to the front legs, I'm working out the elbow position by measuring the span from the shoulder forward.

Adding toe placements...

Adding claw spike geometry...

Toes are already separate capsules so I'll skip extra separation lines, and pads and dewclaws aren't visible so I'll leave those out too. I'm adding fur tufts scattered along the leg surface, filtering by normal direction and height to place them mainly on the back of the upper legs.

Now I'm applying the same tuft logic across the main body surface, scattering a larger number of cards filtered by upward-facing normals, with a steeper lean angle so they flow back and down along the body to mimic natural fur direction.

I'm checking the math on hit density for the body and neck areas to make sure the scatter count stays below the max achievable given minimum spacing, then planning a neck ruff with looser, longer cards plus a dorsal mane strip running along the ridge of the neck and withers.

I'm trying to figure out the exact API semantics for placing frames along the neck tube path, since I'm unsure whether the function returns the collected frames directly or needs a callback to build the array manually.

Deciding to just loop manually, sampling points along the tube at varying parameters with angles spread across three rows (-40°, 0°, 40°) to build a fuller standing mane. I'm planning ridge cards with larger spike sizes leaning backward for flow, using a darker tufted texture, plus cheek ruff cards scattered across the skull surface filtered by position and surface normal to avoid placing them on the front face.

Now I'm adding cheek ruff orientation details, tail cards, and a chest ruff built from a second scatter pass on the body mesh filtered by normal direction to separate front chest hair from the rest, including a cream-colored bib patch using its own filter and density settings. I'm starting to define the skull geometry as a sphere part attached to the head bone with specific scale values for the head shape.

Now I'm sweeping a muzzle shape between two points with a tapering radius function, confirming the tuple typing works correctly through contextual inference, then placing a nose pad sphere at the muzzle tip with its own scale and color.

I'm checking the geometry overlap between the muzzle end and nose pad front faces to make sure the nose protrudes slightly, then placing symmetric nostril spheres and nudging their position inward so they sit flush rather than poking through the nose surface.

Adding a glossy spec highlight to the nose, then sweeping the jaw shape tapering from the chin toward the cheek with cream-colored lit paint.

I'm double-checking that the muzzle and jaw silhouettes meet seamlessly at both the start and end points, verifying the radii line up so there's no visible gap or overlap, and now comparing their lateral widths to make sure the jaw tucks properly behind the muzzle.

I'm figuring out the lip line sweep angles based on the muzzle's facing direction, confirming the sign convention for left versus right sides, then setting up the sweep call with the right thickness and rounded caps for a smooth lip contour. Now I'm moving on to building the upper fangs as cone geometry.

Placing the fang tip pointing outward along the surface normal while the base embeds into the muzzle by a fraction of its height, adjusting angle so the fang points down-and-out slightly, then sizing it appropriately before moving to the lower canines seated on the jaw.

For the lower canines, I decide to skip them since the upper muzzle covers them. Then I move to building the eyes — placing a small dark sphere on the head bone at a lateral offset, scaled uniformly, and adding a decal for the eye highlight pointed outward and slightly up.

For the decal position, I compute the surface point by normalizing the direction vector and offsetting from the eyeball center, setting the decal's direction, size, and mirroring based on which side (left vs right) matches my intended drawing orientation.

I'm narrowing the eye decal width so it stays within the sphere's silhouette and doesn't project oddly onto the skull beyond the eyeball, then adding a brow ridge capsule above each eye for definition.

Checking the brow placement: the lower edge should slightly overhang the eye's top edge to act like a lid, and I'm aligning the lateral endpoints so the brow sits correctly outboard of the eye center.

Now I'm setting up the brow as a tapered capsule shape attached to the head bone, then moving on to whiskers — defining starting points along the muzzle surface and sweeping tapered rods out to tapered tips with pointed caps for each whisker strand.

Next I'm working on the ear joints: placing hinge joints on the head at symmetric lateral positions, computing rotation vectors for ear orientation, and preparing to extrude the ear shape along those axes.

Still working out ear thickness geometry...

Still working through the geometry math...

Skipping that detail, I move to the neck collar: a lathed ring shape positioned at the second neck joint, aligned to its axis with a rivet-styled paint, checking that the radius profile tapers sensibly along the neck's joint keys.

Settling on the collar outline coordinates, I'm noting the neck's bend relative to the joint axis only shifts things a few millimeters, and the tapering radius change across the collar is negligible. Now I'm starting to define a leather paint shader that checks stitch positions along the surface coordinates.

Still writing shader logic...

Darker belt edges past a radius threshold, then placing brass stud spheres in a ring around each joint using outward-facing stick embedding.

I'm figuring out the front collar plate: positioning it via surface-around placement, adding a wide brass box plate, then embedding a small ruby-colored gem sphere centered on that plate's face.

For the pendant below it, I'm computing a base point offset from the plate in world coordinates and extending a fang-colored spike downward from there to form a drop ornament, keeping the shape flat at the top and pointed at the bottom.

Then I'm adding a brass torus ring at the plate's base, oriented so the hole faces front-to-back like a loop a cord could pass through. For the actual fang pendant, I'm sweeping a curved path through a few control points with a tapering radius, flat at the top and coming to a point at the bottom.

Now I'm wrapping a small brass band ring around the fang near its top, oriented horizontally around the shape. For the tail, I'm working out a gradient coat that darkens toward the tip, building it off a countershaded base paint.

I'm considering whether to add further armor touches, like a leather bracer on a foreleg, but deciding most extra details aren't needed right now.

Working out the bracer placement along the leg chain between elbow and wrist, picking a parameter t around .76 so radius interpolates to roughly .0545, then setting inner/outer radii of .050/.068 for the lathe profile.

I'm attaching the bracer rigidly to the elbow joint's bone weighting rather than smooth skinning, and planning to mirror it onto both front legs. For decoration I'm considering adding a small brass stud or ring detail on the bracer surface using a ring primitive aligned to the leg's tangent axis.

Beyond that I'm settling on explicit bone binding so the stud ring stays locked to the elbow during animation, and noting the collar ring just needs its frame centered at the joint position to line up correctly. I still want to add a bit more surface detail like a darker saddle marking across the back and shoulders.

Checking floor contact now — toes, claws, and pads all sit right at y=0, and nothing dips below the ground plane. I'm sketching out the part count (roughly 120 meshes between body, toes, claws, and joints) and confirming triangle counts stay reasonable, then moving to write a closure-based helper function for building the paw geometry inside the main build routine.

Writing paw builder function...
